catalog_quote: HT has two degrees of stress: primary and secondary. Stress is assigned from right to left. Primary stress may fall on the ultimate, penultimate, or antepenultimate syllable of the word, depending on syllable codas, word length, and word class. Secondary stress is assigned to alternate syllables in the morphological word, moving from right to left starting at the syllable bearing primary stress. The primary stress rule is as follows: stress the final syllable if it ends in a sonorant (i.e., moraic)47 consonant or glide, otherwise, stress the penult. ... An alternative way to state the stress rule is to specify that primary stress falls on the final syllable only if that syllable has a moraic coda; otherwise, stress falls on the penult (or antepenult in the case of some nominalized forms, see section 2.5.1.4). ... What is interesting and unique about the HT stress pattern is that the heavy opened syllable CVV behaves like the light syllables CV and CVO with respect to stress assignment in that none of these three syllable types attracts primary stress. Only the heavy closed syllable CVS attracts primary stress.
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.rule_in_words: Right-edge, quantity-sensitive: in native non-ideophonic words (verbs, adjectives, adverbs, nouns alike) primary stress is final if the last syllable is closed by a sonorant consonant or glide (/m n l (r) h ʔ w j/, i.e. a moraic coda = CVS), otherwise penultimate; final CVV, CV-obstruent and CV do not attract stress (long vowels do not count as heavy for stress, which Kung flags as typologically unusual).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Secondary stress on alternate syllables right-to-left starting from the primary-stressed syllable, within the morphological word; assigned after /h/-deletion (primary stress > h-deletion > secondary stress, pp.106-107); extrametrical prefixes may carry secondary stress, the nominalizer -ti never does; in ideophones secondary stress falls on every syllable after the initial primary.
new_statements.exceptions: Extrametrical morphemes that cannot bear primary stress: body-part prefixes, 3PL subject ta-, 3PL object lak-, instrumental paa-, nominalizer -ti (yielding antepenultimate stress in some nominalized nouns, §2.5.1.4); monosyllabic verbs are stressed even if obstruent-final (p.108); ideophonic adverbs have word-initial primary stress (§2.5.2 p.122); Spanish loans keep the stress of the Spanish source syllable (§2.5.3 p.123); lhqapan 'horse' keeps ideophone-initial stress and xtiilan 'green cockroach' is declared lexically stressed (p.122); stress shift marks some derivational pairs (§2.2.3.4 p.65, §4.1.1.3 p.352). Herrera Zendejas 2021 (Mecapalapa variety) states the same final-if-heavy-else-penult rule but counts a final long vowel as heavy.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level rule stated over the morphological word (prefixes+stem+suffixes; clitics such as +t/+ch shown outside the stress domain in transcriptions); examples are citation forms with primary (ˈ) and secondary (ˌ) marks. Herrera Zendejas 2021 adds that stress is 'predictable and non-contrastive' and that f0 is its most consistent acoustic correlate.
new_statements.identity_note: Kung 2007 describes the Tepehua of Huehuetla, Hidalgo (autonym Lhiimaqalhqama') = hueh1236 exactly. Herrera Zendejas 2021 (JIPA) describes Mecapalapa Tepehua (Pantepec, Puebla), spoken by descendants of 19th-century migrants from Huehuetla and classed under the same ISO code tee / Huehuetla branch, so it also falls under hueh1236; its stress rule agrees with Kung's except that it treats a final long vowel as heavy. Watters 1980 (also saved) is Tlachichilco Tepehua, a different Glottolog language (tlac1235), kept only for comparison. No Tepehua language is currently in the catalog (only Tepehuan, Uto-Aztecan, which is unrelated).

new_statements.rule_in_words: Native words (verbs, adjectives, non-ideophonic adverbs, nouns): primary stress on the final syllable if it is closed by a sonorant consonant or glide (/m n l r ʔ h w j/, which are moraic in coda), otherwise on the penult; antepenult in some nominalized forms. Weight is coda-based only: CVV, CV and obstruent-closed CVO do not attract stress, only sonorant-closed CVS. Ideophones: primary stress on the first syllable. Spanish loans: stress where the Spanish source has it.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Native words: secondary stress on alternate syllables of the morphological word, right to left, starting from the primary-stressed syllable (assigned after /h/-deletion, which follows primary stress assignment). Ideophones: secondary stress on all subsequent syllables left to right. Loanwords: alternate syllables right to left from the primary. Body-part prefixes, ta-, lak- and paa- may bear secondary stress; the nominalizing suffix -ti never does.
new_statements.exceptions: Extrametrical morphemes that may not bear primary stress: body-part prefixes, 3pl subject ta- and object lak-, instrumental paa-, nominalizer -ti. Antepenultimate stress in some nominalized forms (§2.5.1.4). Ideophonic adverbs take initial stress (§2.5.2); Spanish loanwords keep the Spanish stress position (§2.5.3). Glottalized /p' t' k'/ do not add weight; rhotics: no evidence either way (n.48). Primary-stressed vowels are phonetically lengthened regardless of phonemic length (p.51 n.17).
new_statements.identity_note: Kung's data are from the town of Huehuetla, Hidalgo (fieldwork June 1999 to July 2005); she treats the Mecapalapa (Puebla) speech as an immigrant offshoot of Huehuetla Tepehua. Kryder 1987 also worked in Huehuetla (fieldwork from 1984, per Kung p.68). The Herrera Zendejas 2021 JIPA illustration already in this folder describes the Mecapalapa variety; Watters 1980 describes Tlachichilco Tepehua (tlac1235), a different language.

Compatible with the existing Kung 2007 statement (right-to-left, ultimate vs penultimate depending on codas and word class): Kryder's finals-attracting set /ʔ h w y l ɬ/ matches Kung's glide/sonorant codas, and her vowel-final and /t/-final penults match Kung's 'otherwise penult'. new_statements.rule_in_words: No formal rule is stated (author explicitly defers one); observationally, primary stress is on the final syllable in 366 of 415 recorded lexical items and on the penult in the other 49. Final stress is regular when the word ends in /p, č, c̓, q, ʔ, h, l, ɬ, w, y/; penultimate stress clusters in vowel-final words (25/49, almost all short vowels) and /t/-final words (17/49). Word class matters: bare verb stems are oxytone, related noun stems paroxytone (kuštú 'work in the cornfield' vs kúštu 'cornfield'). Certain word-final inflectional suffixes always take primary stress (-ni(n), -yan, -yá', -ya, -nV', -nin, -nVn, -tit [listed], -'an, -nin 'plural'); the second vowel of polysyllabic -čo'ó 'iterative' and -palá 'durative' is stressed; -ti, -tit, -ta and preterit -ɬi are never stressed. Clitics are never stressed; Spanish loans keep Spanish stress. i.e. right-edge stress, final vs penultimate conditioned by the final segment and by morphology/word class.
new_statements.secondary_stress: None described: only the single loudest syllable is marked ('I have left other syllables unmarked').
new_statements.exceptions: 49 paroxytones out of 415 (vowel-final, /t/-final, a few in /k s š n/); noun/verb stress pairs (kúštu/kuštú, pápa 'husband' / papá' 'male'); unstressable suffixes -ti, -tit, -ta, -ɬi; clitics never stressed; Spanish loanwords follow the Spanish pattern (Appendix 1).
new_statements.identity_note: Kryder 1987 is titled simply 'Tepehua' but the three consultants were born in Huehuetla, Hidalgo (recorded in Mecapalapa, Puebla, 1984, and Huehuetla, Dec 1985), so it describes Huehuetla Tepehua (hueh1236), the same variety as Kung 2007; Mecapalapa is the Puebla settlement of Huehuetla speakers also described by Herrera Zendejas 2021.

sources.note: Section 'Word stress' pp.300-301: 'Stress is predictable and non-contrastive in MT. It falls on either the penultimate or on the rightmost syllable, being sensitive to syllable weight. Word-final stress occurs if the last syllable is heavy. If this is not the case, penultimate syllables are stressed. Final syllables count as heavy if they have a long vowel or if they have a short vowel closed by a nasal, glide, lateral or glottal stop.' Word-final obstruent codas count as light.
